name: Why the night shift stopped at the jute press
subject: history
question: cause
brief: Your history folder holds three short extracts about a two-day walkout by the night shift at a jute baling press on the Hooghly in the 1930s: the manager's telegram, a thumb-marked petition from the workers and a municipal boiler inspector's note. Only one printed set was made for your table, and every further document means a trip to the library. You are the author, drafting the group's explanation of why the night shift stopped work.

claims.name: The shift stopped because a new weigh-clerk docked every bale for damp without weighing it again
The refusal of the customary advance before Puja turned a quarrel at the scales into a stoppage
The shift left the shed because the main boiler burst

evidence.name: Clause 1 of the petition names the new weigh-clerk and protests a flat deduction of four seers a bale for damp
The inspector's margin note says the baling scales still carried the chalk mark for the four-seer deduction
Clause 3 of the petition says the cashier closed his grating on Tuesday without paying the customary advance
The manager's telegram asks head office for authority to pay half the festival advance 'to bring the night hands back'
The inspector certifies that both boilers held normal working pressure throughout the week
The export bales were stencilled in black ink for shipment from the docks

limitations.name: The weigh-clerk's own account to the labour officer is not in the packet
The petition was drafted in English by a petition-writer in the bazaar, not in the workers' own words
The papers cover only one shed and do not show whether the day shift shared the grievance

note: Set in the history classroom at Nabapara Vidyalaya (loc_nhss); the walkout and its papers are an invented teaching set, not a record of a real mill. A strike with two causes is ordinary history, so two claims are defensible. The boiler claim is contradicted by the inspector's certificate. The stencil colour is beside the point.
